newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila says Subic row won't hit foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: Manila says Subic row won't hit foreign investment.

text.p: The cancellation of bidding for a container port terminal in Subic Bay will not scare away foreign investors from the Philippines, an aide to President Fidel Ramos said on Friday.
"I think the decision would not scare but rather attract them more...That is the best that could have been done under the premises," presidential legal adviser Renato Cayetano told reporters.

Ramos cancelled the bidding on Thursday and ordered the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA) not to enter into a contract with Hutchison Ports Philippines Limited, a unit of Hong Kong's Hutchison Whampoa.
SBMA has recommended awarding the project to Hutchison after bidding last year.

"We have found the terms of reference provided in the tender document to have been disregarded by the SBMA Bids and Awards Committee in its determination of the winning bid," Ramos said in a letter to SBMA chairman Richard Gordon, which was made public.
Economists and political analysts said the move could dampen foreign investment in the country.

"If you change decisions already made, and there have been many times when this has happened, it puts into question whether the government has firm policies .. the permanence of stability in its decisions," said political analyst Amando Doronila. "It will weaken or undermine confidence in our business procedures."
Cayetano said it was better to order re-bidding rather than award the project unilaterally.

"It was the feeling of the committee that reviewed this whole process that even the bidders themselves were rather confused and misinformed as to what exactly are the definite parameters of the bidding," he said.
The Subic project became controversial when Philippine port operator International Container Terminal Services (ICTSI) protested after being edged out in the bidding.
Ramos then ordered a review of the process.

SBMA rejected ICTSI's original bid on the grounds that it would violate a law forbidding monopolies in the port industry. ICTSI operates the Manila International Container Terminal, which handles 70 percent of container traffic in the country.

It said it also rejected ICTSI's contention that the only financial factor to be looked into was royalty per twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU). In the original bidding in August, ICTSI gave the highest royalty of $58 per TEU, followed by Hutchison with $20.50 and Germany's Royal Port Services with $15.00.
But Hutchison had promised to build more wharfs at Subic in the fourth year of the 25-year contract, as compared to the ninth year proposed by ICTSI.

ICTSI officials expressed satisfaction on the decision of Ramos to order fresh bidding on the project. ICTSI is "pleased with this new development (and) expresses hope that the controversy can now be laid to rest," a company statement said.
ICTSI intends to participate in the re-bidding, the statement added.
